title: Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard: FMVSS No. 135; Modernization to Accommodate Automated Driving Systems-Equipped Vehicles
pass_4_primary_concern: The proposal picks left-side substitution as the default for ADS-only vehicles without fully explaining why that rule works best across unconventional layouts.
pass_5_high_stakes_domain_reason: The proposal amends a federal motor vehicle safety standard governing braking systems, so its implementation affects safety-critical compliance for vehicles operating on public roads.
pass_5_concise_why: Coherent, but the default choice and burden savings are underexplained.
pass_5_most_important_consequence: If the chosen default location or on-board-actuation wording is too rigid, ADS-only vehicles could face avoidable compliance ambiguity or extra review work before the rule is fully effective.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The proposal makes the control-definition and actuation changes before the real-world stop-request pathway is fully described.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask NHTSA to sequence the user-pathway description before finalizing the control wording.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The proposal changes a safety rule for ADS-only vehicles while offering limited comparative evidence in the notice text for why the new default and the no-harm conclusion are adequate.

evidence.quote_or_absence: The notice states that the rule would remove unnecessary regulatory burdens and costs without detriment to vehicle safety, but it does not supply a comparative example set or quantified support in the excerpt.

pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask for the concrete basis for the claimed no-safety-disbenefit result.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The remedy fits the problem in broad terms, but the justification for choosing one default substitute location remains thin.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask why the chosen remedy is better than a more flexible location rule.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The proposal is implementable, but the excerpt leaves open whether all brake-by-wire variants will map cleanly onto the new definitions.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask for examples covering complex or distributed brake architectures.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The notice downplays impacts, but the residual burden and practical compliance effects are not shown to be negligible.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask for an estimate of the remaining certification and compliance work.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule leaves edge-case fallback behavior and correction paths only lightly specified.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask whether the final text needs a clearer fallback or correction process.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The proposal likely shifts some clarification work downstream to manufacturers and reviewers, but the notice does not separate that burden from the claimed simplification.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask how much work the amendment shifts to later certification review.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The amended control definitions can still create a certification gateway for atypical vehicles, though the notice does not show it is severe.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask how many platforms would still need special review after the amendment.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: Safety, cost, design clarity, and certification consequences are not fully separated in the notice's explanation.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask NHTSA to separate those consequence classes in the final rule preamble.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The proposal is coherent, but the causal chain from problem to remedy would be easier to audit if each design choice were linked more explicitly to the safety purpose.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask for a one-to-one mapping between each proposed change and the problem it solves.
